claims.text: Thermal exposure at service temperatures combined with cyclic mechanical loading causes localized atomic ordering at grain boundaries in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Localized grain-boundary ordering facilitates nucleation of incipient brittle intermetallic phases.
The incipient brittle intermetallic phases degrade toughness.
This proposed mechanism is distinct from conventional-alloy behavior dominated by grain-boundary segregation or rapid, extensive intermetallic precipitation.
The initial high-entropy alloy is single-phase and chemically homogeneous, with uniformly distributed elements.
Controlled thermal exposure combined with cyclic loading promotes diffusion and atomic ordering.
Localized atomic ordering at grain boundaries acts as nucleation sites for brittle intermetallic phases.
Sustained thermal and mechanical stress enhances local diffusion kinetics at grain boundaries.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion produces incipient ordering that precedes brittle intermetallic formation.
Grain-boundary brittle intermetallic phases create weak spots responsible for toughness degradation.
Thermomechanically treated samples will have lower fracture toughness than the as-processed baseline.
Treated samples will contain early-stage intermetallic precipitates or ordered domains localized at grain boundaries.
The as-processed baseline lacks grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation.
The as-processed baseline has favorable strength–ductility characteristics.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate service-temperature conditions with cyclic loading.
At very high temperatures or extreme mechanical conditions that cause complete phase transformations, mechanisms other than localized grain-boundary ordering may predominate.
The ordering kinetics, extent of ordering, and toughness decrease depend on alloy composition and service conditions.
